title: Pokot Goat Soup
author: Mama Wanjiru

heritage.origin: West Pokot and Baringo Counties — Rift Valley
heritage.history: The Pokot people inhabit the mountainous region of West Pokot and Baringo. Their goat soup is prepared for celebrations, healing, and communal gatherings. Wild herbs collected from the highlands are incorporated for both flavour and medicinal benefit.
heritage.modernEvolution: Pokot goat soup traditions are maintained within the community with the specific herbs reflecting deep knowledge of local plant ecology.

desc: Pokot Goat Soup — bone-in goat simmered for hours with wild highland herbs, onions, and simple spices into a deeply nourishing, clear, restorative broth. The ceremonial and healing soup of the Pokot people.
longDesc: Pokot goat soup is both sustenance and medicine — prepared for those who are unwell, for mothers after childbirth, for elders, and for ceremonies. The combination of slow-simmered goat bones and wild highland herbs creates a broth of extraordinary depth.
ingredients: 1.5 kg bone-in goat — including neck and knuckle bones
steps: Blanch goat bones: cover with cold water, bring to a boil for 5 minutes, discard water.
In fresh water, combine all ingredients.
Bring to a gentle boil. Reduce to lowest simmer.
Cook for 90—120 minutes until meat falls off bones and broth is deeply flavoured.
Skim foam regularly for a clear broth.
Serve in bowls with meat and broth, garnished with coriander.
chefTips: The blanching step produces a clearer broth — do not skip it.
Wild herbs add the authentic Pokot character.
This soup should be clear golden, not murky.
cookingScience: Long gentle simmering of bones extracts collagen, converting it to gelatin that gives the broth its silky body.
sustainabilityTips: Using goat bones that would otherwise be discarded makes full use of the animal.
storage: Refrigerate for up to 4 days. Freeze for 3 months.
culturalNote: Pokot goat soup is more than food — it is medicine and ceremony, representing the deep botanical knowledge of the Pokot people.
